title: CAN YOU LOSE YOUR SALVATION… OR WERE YOU NEVER TRULY SAVED?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOSE YOUR SALVATION… OR WERE YOU NEVER TRULY SAVED?
The terrifying words “I never knew you,” the promise that no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from His hand, and the question that may change how you understand your eternity.
There is a kind of fear that doesn't come when you're standing in a cemetery.
It comes when you're sitting alone, remembering who you used to be.
Or worse…
Remembering what you did last night.
You know the Scriptures. You've prayed the prayers. You've sung about the blood of Jesus, raised your hands in worship, and told people that God changed your life.
But there's something you haven't told anyone.
You still struggle.
Sometimes with the same sin you thought you had buried years ago.

Sometimes you wonder whether your repentance was ever genuine. Whether that moment you surrendered to Christ was real. Whether heaven still has your name written somewhere, or whether you've been holding on to a promise that was never yours.
And then someone quotes Hebrews 6.
Someone else quotes John 10.
One person tells you salvation can never be lost.
Another warns you that a believer can fall away.
And somewhere between their arguments, a wounded soul whispers:
“Jesus… am I still Yours?”
Before you answer that question, there is something you need to understand.
The Bible contains both astonishing promises of security and terrifying warnings against falling away.
Neither should be erased.
Neither should be softened to make our theology more comfortable.
And neither was written to make Jesus seem less trustworthy.
What if the question isn't merely whether you can lose your salvation?
What if the deeper question is whether you've actually understood what it means to belong to Christ?
Because there is a difference between falling into sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between struggling against darkness and choosing to live in it.
And there is a difference between knowing religious language and knowing the Savior Himself.
Jesus said something in Matthew 7:21–23 that should make every religious person examine their heart.
Not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven. Some will point to extraordinary works performed in His name.
And His answer will be devastating:
“I never knew you.” (Matthew 7:23, KJV)
Not “I knew you once.”
Not “I loved you until you made one terrible mistake.”
But “I never knew you.”
The original Greek is striking:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
The word οὐδέποτε (oudepote) means “never” or “not at any time.”
The verb ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.” In this context, Jesus is speaking about a relationship of recognition and belonging, not a lack of information.
He knew exactly who those people were.
But they did not belong to Him as His true disciples.
And here is what makes this passage so unsettling.
These were not people who had necessarily rejected religious activity.
They were people who could point to religious activity as evidence of their acceptance before God.
They had impressive things to say about what they had done in Jesus' name.
But Jesus pointed to something their impressive claims could not conceal.
They were workers of lawlessness.
Their public profession did not correspond to a life surrendered to His authority.
That should disturb anyone who has learned how to look Christian without actually following Christ.
But please hear the distinction.
Jesus was not describing a broken believer who hated their sin and was crying out for mercy.
He was exposing the tragedy of religious profession without genuine obedience and relationship.
And that distinction matters more than you may realize.
Because somewhere right now, a person who genuinely loves Jesus is terrified that one failure has erased years of faith.
Meanwhile, someone else is deliberately living in unrepentant sin, completely unconcerned, because they repeated a prayer when they were twelve.
Both need biblical truth.
But they do not need the same warning.
One needs to remember the mercy of Christ.
The other needs to stop using grace as permission to remain unchanged.
And the Gospel speaks to both.
Think about Peter.
He had walked with Jesus. Heard His teaching. Witnessed His miracles. Declared his loyalty.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine what that third denial must have done to him.
Luke tells us that the Lord turned and looked directly at Peter.
Then Peter remembered what Jesus had said.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that walk?
The shame.
The sound of his own voice still echoing in his memory.
The unbearable realization that he had denied the One he loved.
If salvation depended on never failing catastrophically, what hope would Peter have had?
But before Peter ever fell, Jesus had already told him:
“I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.” (Luke 22:32, KJV)
Jesus did not say Peter would never stumble.
He foretold the coming trial and prayed for Peter's faith.
And after the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus restored Peter through a deeply personal encounter.
Three denials.
Then a conversation in which Jesus repeatedly asked Peter about his love and entrusted him with caring for His sheep.
The man who had once denied knowing Jesus would later stand publicly and proclaim Him.
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance was real.
And Christ's restoring grace was real.
But don't misunderstand Peter's story.
His restoration is not permission to deny Jesus whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
It is evidence that a terrible fall does not automatically mean Christ is finished with a repentant disciple.
The same Savior who confronted Peter's failure also restored him to faithful service.
Now consider Judas.
He, too, had walked with Jesus.
He had heard the teaching.
He had been among the Twelve.
He had participated in a ministry that changed lives.
Yet John 6:64 tells us that Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray Him.
Judas' proximity to Jesus did not equal saving faith.
His outward position concealed an inward unbelief.
Peter fell terribly and was restored.
Judas betrayed Jesus and died in despair.
These two stories do not provide a complete formula for diagnosing every person's spiritual condition. But together they expose something essential.
Being close to Christian things is not the same as belonging to Christ.
A church position cannot save you.
A ministry title cannot save you.
A Christian family cannot save you.
An emotional altar experience, by itself, cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
And genuine faith receives Him, rather than merely borrowing His name.
Now we arrive at one of the most comforting promises in all of Scripture.
Jesus says in John 10:27–28:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” (KJV)
Read that slowly.
Jesus does not describe eternal life as wages His sheep must earn.
He says He gives it.
The Greek expression translated “they shall never perish” is especially emphatic:
οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
Ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna.
A faithful rendering is:
“They will certainly never perish.”
The combination οὐ μή (ou mē) is a strong form of negation in Greek.
Jesus is giving His sheep an extraordinary assurance.
He continues in John 10:29, teaching that no one is able to snatch them out of His Father's hand.
This is not a weak Savior hoping His people can somehow hold on long enough.
This is the Good Shepherd speaking about His own preserving power.
But notice something that must not be removed from the passage.
Jesus describes His sheep as those who hear His voice and follow Him.
The verbs portray the characteristic relationship between the Shepherd and His sheep.
His sheep listen.
His sheep follow.
Not perfectly.
Not without stumbling.
But genuinely.
The promise is not that someone can permanently reject Christ, embrace rebellion without repentance, and still confidently claim the blessings of discipleship because of a past religious decision.
The promise is that Christ gives eternal life to His sheep, and no enemy can overpower His protecting hand.

Christians have debated whether this passage also rules out every possibility of a believer later abandoning faith. But what no faithful reading should deny is the strength of Jesus' promise or the necessity of following Him.
And that brings us to the passages that many people would rather avoid.

Hebrews 6:4–6 speaks of people who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, become partakers of the Holy Spirit, tasted the goodness of God's word and the powers of the coming age, and then fallen away.
The Greek word translated “fall away” is:
παραπεσόντας
Parapesontas.
It comes from parapiptō, meaning to fall away or commit apostasy.
The warning is severe.
The author speaks of the impossibility of renewing such people again to repentance under the conditions described.
That should never be treated casually.
But what exactly is being described?
Christians who take Scripture seriously have understood this passage differently.
Some understand it as a warning about people who experienced the blessings and powerful realities of the Christian community without ever possessing genuine saving faith.
Others understand it as a warning that genuine believers can decisively turn away from Christ, forfeiting the salvation they once possessed.
Still others emphasize that the warning itself is one of the means God uses to keep His people persevering in faith.
These interpretations differ significantly.
It would be misleading to pretend the Greek language alone settles the entire disagreement.
But the central warning is unmistakable.
Do not turn away from Jesus Christ.
Do not treat His sacrifice as something disposable.
Do not presume that outward spiritual experiences make repentance unnecessary.
And do not imagine that a heart hardened against Christ is a harmless condition.
Hebrews 10:26–27 adds another sobering warning about deliberate sin after receiving the knowledge of the truth.
The passage must be read in its context, where rejecting Christ's sacrifice and turning away from Him are central concerns.
It should not be reduced to the claim that any intentional sin committed by a Christian makes forgiveness impossible.
If that were the meaning, the New Testament's repeated calls for believers to confess, repent, and receive mercy would become difficult to reconcile.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
The Greek verb for “confess” is:
ὁμολογῶμεν
Homologōmen.
It comes from homologeō, meaning to acknowledge or confess.
Biblical confession is not merely reciting an apology while secretly planning to continue in rebellion.
It involves bringing sin into the light and agreeing with God's judgment about it.
And true repentance involves turning toward God rather than defending the darkness.
Does that mean a genuine believer never falls into the same sin twice?
No.
It means we must never redefine repentance as permission to stop fighting.
There is a world of difference between a person who says, “Lord, I hate what I have done. Help me turn away,” and a person who says, “God has to forgive me, so I have no reason to change.”
One is seeking mercy.
The other is presuming upon it.
And only God sees the human heart perfectly.
This is where 1 John 2:19 becomes important.
John writes about people who departed from the believing community:
“They went out from us, but they were not of us…” (KJV)
He explains that their departure revealed that they did not truly belong to the fellowship in the sense he was describing.
This passage strongly supports the understanding that some apparent believers were never genuinely Christ's.
But we must read it honestly.
John was addressing a particular departure involving false teaching and opposition to apostolic truth.
His statement should not be carelessly turned into a verdict that every person who struggles, experiences doubt, changes churches, or goes through a spiritual crisis was never saved.
That would go beyond what the passage establishes.
Still, it raises a piercing question.
Can someone appear Christian for years without truly belonging to Christ?
Yes.
Jesus' parable of the soils in Matthew 13 shows that some receive the word with initial joy but do not endure when trouble or persecution comes.
Other lives become unfruitful because the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word.
Not every visible beginning produces lasting fruit.
And this should humble us.
Because the most dangerous deception is not always someone pretending to believe while knowing they are pretending.
Sometimes it is a person sincerely assuming they belong to Christ while never having surrendered to Him.
They love the atmosphere of worship.
They love the friendships.
They love the blessings.
They love the idea of heaven.
But they do not want Jesus to rule their lives.
They want forgiveness without repentance.
A Savior without a Lord.
A cross without dying to self.
A crown without following the King.
Yet Jesus calls His disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him (Luke 9:23).
Not to purchase salvation through suffering.
But because saving faith unites us to a Savior who transforms those who belong to Him.
And this brings us to another truth that cannot be compromised.
We are saved by grace, not by our performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Greek word for grace is:
χάρις
Charis.
Grace speaks of favor freely given, not wages earned by deserving sinners.
And Paul continues in Ephesians 2:10 by saying believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for them to walk in.
Do you see the order?
Grace comes first.
Salvation is God's gift.
Good works are its intended fruit, not its purchase price.
We do not obey Jesus to make His cross sufficient.
We obey because the crucified and risen Christ has called us into new life.
The person who says, “My obedience makes me worthy of salvation,” has misunderstood grace.
But the person who says, “Grace means my obedience doesn't matter,” has misunderstood grace too.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace does more than pardon.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace does not leave the repentant sinner where it found them.
That transformation may involve a long, painful battle.
There may be setbacks.
There may be tears no one sees.
There may be years of learning to surrender wounds, habits, fears, and desires to Christ.
But the direction of genuine discipleship is toward Him.
Not toward celebrating the sin from which He came to redeem us.
Now listen to the words of Paul in Philippians 1:6:
“Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
Paul's confidence is rooted in God's faithful work.
And Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor the powers Paul names, nor anything else in creation will be able to separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
These are not small promises.
They are meant to strengthen Christians in suffering, persecution, weakness, and uncertainty.
At the same time, Romans 11:20–22 warns against arrogance and unbelief, and urges continued faith in God's kindness.
Colossians 1:22–23 connects the hope of final reconciliation with continuing in the faith.
And Hebrews 3:14 speaks of sharing in Christ if we hold our original confidence firmly to the end.
The New Testament refuses to separate assurance from perseverance.
This is why faithful Christians have developed two major understandings of the relationship between salvation and apostasy.

Those who hold to the perseverance of the saints teach that everyone truly regenerated by God's grace will ultimately be preserved in faith. Some who appear to fall away permanently, they argue, never possessed saving faith in the first place.
Those who hold to conditional security teach that genuine believers must continue in living faith and that deliberate, final apostasy can result in forfeiting salvation.
Both traditions appeal to Scripture.
Both affirm that salvation comes through Jesus Christ rather than human merit.
Both warn against unbelief and persistent rebellion.
Both recognize the necessity of God's grace.
Their disagreement is real, and it should not be disguised.
But here is something extraordinary.

Whether someone believes genuine salvation cannot finally be lost, or that genuine believers must continue in faith to remain in Christ, neither position gives anyone biblical permission to abandon Jesus.
And neither requires a repentant believer to believe that Christ is unwilling to receive them.
The invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Trust Christ.
Abide in Christ.
Repent when you sin.
Do not harden your heart.
Do not place your confidence in your religious résumé.
And do not make your failures greater than the mercy of the Savior.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What an astonishing invitation.
Not “Whoever comes with a perfect record.”
Not “Whoever has never doubted.”
Not “Whoever has never cried over the same weakness twice.”
Whoever comes to Him.
That is not a promise that repentance is unnecessary.
It is a promise that the Savior is not reluctant to receive those who truly come.
Maybe you've been reading this while carrying a secret.
An addiction you keep hiding.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
Bitterness you have fed for years.
A double life.
A prayer life that has become almost nonexistent.
A faith that looks alive in public but feels painfully distant in private.
Maybe you're frightened because you know you've been drifting.
Or maybe you're exhausted because you've been fighting for so long that you wonder whether the struggle itself means you're not saved.
Please understand something.
Your feelings alone cannot determine your spiritual condition.
Feeling afraid does not prove you are lost.
Feeling confident does not prove you are saved.
A past profession, by itself, does not settle every question.
And a season of painful struggle, by itself, does not establish that you have been abandoned by God.
Scripture directs us to Christ, His promises, the reality of faith, and the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
Second Corinthians 13:5 tells believers to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith.
That is a serious command.
But biblical self-examination is not meant to become an endless prison of self-obsession.
It should lead us toward the truth.
And ultimately toward Jesus.
Ask yourself:
Am I trusting the finished work of Jesus Christ, or am I trusting a religious experience?
When God's Word confronts my sin, do I seek repentance, or do I continually justify my rebellion?
Do I desire Christ Himself, or only the benefits I hope He will give me?
Am I willing to follow Him even when obedience costs me something?
When I fall, do I return to Him for mercy and transformation?
These questions are not a mechanical test that can reveal the heart with God's perfect knowledge.
They are invitations to examine whether our profession of faith is matched by a genuine response to the Savior.
And if your conscience is accusing you right now, don't stop at accusation.
Listen to 1 John 2:1.
John writes so that believers may not sin, but adds that if anyone does sin, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” (KJV)
An advocate.
Not an excuse for sin.
An advocate for sinners.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
The One who never sinned is the One through whom repentant sinners receive mercy.
The Gospel is not the story of good people successfully protecting their spotless records.
It is the story of the holy Son of God entering a fallen world, bearing sin, dying on the cross, and rising again so that sinners might be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
He was not crucified because sin was harmless.
He was crucified because sin is deadly serious.
And He did not rise from the grave merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He rose as the victorious Savior and Lord.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is the appropriate response of a heart turning to the God who gives grace.
The Greek word often translated “repentance” is:
μετάνοια
Metanoia.
It denotes a change of mind or understanding, and in the New Testament's call to repentance, that change is inseparable from turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not simply feeling guilty.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance is more than emotional pain over consequences.
It is a Godward turning.
A surrender of excuses.
A willingness to come into the light.
A desire for the life that Christ commands and gives.
And if you're wondering whether you have already wandered too far, remember the father in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son.
The younger son had wasted his inheritance in reckless living.
He had dishonored his father.
He had brought himself into misery.
And when he came to himself, he decided to return.
Luke 15:20 tells us that while the son was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
Picture that moment.
A son expecting humiliation.
A father running with compassion.
A confession beginning.
An embrace already given.
The father did not pretend the rebellion was righteous.
But he welcomed the returning son.
And celebration followed.
The parable is not a technical proof that settles every theological dispute about whether salvation can be lost.
Jesus told it in the context of God's joy over repentant sinners.
And its message of mercy is breathtaking.
God is not indifferent to repentance.
He welcomes sinners who turn to Him.
Maybe that is the picture your heart needs tonight.
Not a God who approves of your rebellion.
Not a God who is deceived by religious appearances.
But a holy and merciful Father who calls sinners home.
And a Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who truly comes to Him.
Some of you need to stop living as though one confessed failure has placed you beyond the reach of Christ.
Others need to stop living as though a prayer from years ago gives you permission to reject His commands today.
Some need comfort.
Some need confrontation.
Some need to confess what they have been hiding.
Some need to ask forgiveness from the people they have wounded.
Some need to walk away from a sin they have spent years defending.
And some need, for the first time, to surrender to Jesus rather than merely admire Him.
Whatever your situation, do not let this become another article that briefly moves your emotions and leaves your life unchanged.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray with honesty.
Seek mature, biblically grounded counsel if you are confused or overwhelmed.
Bring your sin into the light.
And remember that the Christian life is not sustained by pretending to be stronger than you are.
It is sustained by the grace of God, through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.
If you're returning to God after a season of rebellion, you can write “No more hiding.”
If you need prayer, simply say “Pray for me.” You do not have to reveal painful personal details to strangers to be worthy of prayer.
And if Christ has restored you after a terrible failure, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy. Someone reading may believe that their own story is beyond redemption.
Your honesty could help them look toward the Savior.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around fear.
Not to turn every weakness into a sensational headline.
And certainly not to replace your local church, your pastor, or the fellowship of believers who can walk beside you in real life.
We want to keep pointing people back to the Scriptures, back to repentance, back to grace, and above all, back to Jesus Christ.
Because somewhere there is a father who thinks his failures have ruined his family forever.
A mother who cries after everyone else has gone to sleep.
A young person who knows how to smile in church while secretly drowning in shame.
A former believer who wonders whether there is any way home.
And a religious person who has never truly understood the Gospel despite years of attending services.
These are not merely audiences or numbers.
They are people who need the truth of Christ.
And consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting others to follow for continuing biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources.
These resources are intended to help make biblical learning more accessible, especially for people who may not have the means to purchase every book they need.
But making Christian resources available, developing new teaching materials, and expanding the reach of Gospel-centered content require ongoing work and practical support.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and sincere, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not need to send money to receive His forgiveness.
It is simply a practical expression of appreciation for people who voluntarily help sustain the work.
Because the goal is not to gather people around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus.
And now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
Can you lose your salvation, or were you never truly saved?
The Christian church has long disagreed over how certain passages answer that precise question.
We should not pretend otherwise.
But the Scriptures leave us with truths that are too important to miss.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
It is received by grace through faith, not earned through human achievement.
An outward profession of faith can exist without genuine conversion.
A genuine follower of Christ can fall into grievous sin and need restoration.
Persistent unbelief and apostasy are matters of eternal seriousness.
The warnings of Scripture must be heard.
The promises of Christ must be trusted.
And everyone who truly comes to Jesus finds a Savior who does not turn away the repentant sinner.
So don't spend your entire life arguing about whether a person can lose salvation while neglecting the Savior who gives it.
Don't build your assurance on the memory of a prayer while refusing to listen to His voice.
And don't spend your nights measuring your failures as though they were more powerful than His cross.
Look to Jesus.
The crucified Jesus.
The risen Jesus.
The Jesus who called Peter back after his denial.
The Jesus who warned religious hypocrites.
The Jesus who receives sinners.
The Jesus who calls His sheep to hear His voice and follow Him.
If you've never truly trusted Him, come to Him.
If you've wandered, repent and return.
If you've fallen, confess your sin and seek His mercy.
If you're walking with Him through weakness, continue trusting His grace.
And if you've been using religion to hide an unsurrendered heart, stop hiding.
Because eternity is too serious for counterfeit faith.
And the love of Christ is too wonderful to treat as something ordinary.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony before you come to Him.
You need the Savior.
The One who knows the whole truth about you.
The One whose death and resurrection are the foundation of Christian hope.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
Perhaps the most important question is not whether you can remember the exact day you first said you believed.
Perhaps it is this:
When Jesus calls you to Himself today, are you willing to trust Him, turn from sin, and follow Him?
Don't answer for the people watching.
Don't answer for your reputation.
Answer before God.
And remember this:
Your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter when you bring your life to Jesus Christ.
